articles.title: Constrained partnership
articles.content: “Trust takes years to build, seconds to break, and forever to repair.”Anonymous THIS observation aptly describes Pakistan’s relationship with one of its most important international health partners. Since 2003, the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria has disbursed more than $1.1 billion to Pakistan’s HIV, tuberculosis and malaria programmes. In August 2020, however, itinvokedits Additional Safeguard Policy (ASP) on Pakistan. Behind this bureaucratic terminology lies an extraordinary decision: the Global Fund no longer had sufficient confidence in the country’s arrangements for managing its grants and implementing disease-control programmes. More than six years later, this decision deserves serious public scrutiny. Established in 2002, the Global Fund is one of the most successful innovations in international health financing. It mobilises resources to support countries fighting these three diseases and has helped save an estimated 72 million lives globally. Pakistan has been a significant beneficiary. The Global Fund normally operates through a partnership model in which national stakeholders identify priorities, nominate implementing organisations and oversee grants through a Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM). The underlying philosophy is country ownership: international resources should strengthen national institutions, not substitute for them. The Global Fund’s observations point to serious weaknesses in governance & institutional accountability. In 2004, the Global Fund Board adopted ASP to address situations where normal funding arrangements could not adequately protect its investments. It permits oversight and direct involvement in selecting principal recipients and implementing partners. In effect, decisions normally taken by national institutions can be assumed by the international financing agency. This is an exceptional, temporary arrangement, reflecting serious concerns about governance, institutional capacity, accountability or programme implementation. Since its introduction, it has been invoked in around 30 countries but revoked in only three: Cuba, Myanmar and Côte d’Ivoire. This shows that entering ASP is easier than exiting it. Why was Pakistan placed under ASP? The answer lies in a candid letter dated Aug 6, 2020, from the Global Fund to the Pakistan government. It expressed serious dissatisfaction with Pakistan’s response to HIV and TB, noting stagnating or declining TB notifications and an almost unchecked increase in HIV incidence. Significantly, it stated that public-sector principal recipients had failed to translate domestic and external financing into effective programmes. The letter specifically criticised the performance of the Common Management Unit (CMU), responsible for coordinating the three disease programmes, and identified inadequate leadership in managing challenges arising from devolution. These observations point to serious weaknesses in governance, leadership, coordination and institutional accountability. Consider this: Between 2020 and 2022, Pakistan changed the national coordinator of the CMU 10 times in three years. Many appointments were political. The epidemiological consequences are equally troubling. While many states have reduced new HIV infections, Pakistan has moved in the opposite direction. According to WHO and UNAIDS estimates reported in Dec 2025, annual new infectionsincreasedfrom approximately 16,000 in 2010 to 48,000 in 2024 — a 200pc increase. ASP’s implications extend beyond these programmes. For a country seeking international investment, development assistance and credibility in global institutions, its inability to demonstrate satisfactory governance of externally financed health programmes sends a deeply damaging message. But ASP should not be viewed merely as an international embarrassment. Its more serious implication is the erosion of national ownership. When external partners increasingly determine arrangements, domestic institutions risk becoming less accountable for results. Pakistan must therefore develop a credible, time-bound roadmap for exiting ASP. The Aug 2020 letter identified the conditions for its revocation: timely provincial budget disbursements for HIV and TB; satisfactory programme performance and financial risk management; demonstrated political commitment; compliance with audit recommendations, etc. Federal and provincial governments must jointly establish a high-level mechanism to monitor progress against each condition through independently verifiable indicators. Civil society and affected communities must also be meaningfully engaged. There is another dimension requiring urgent attention: financial sustainability. For over two decades, Pakistan has depended heavily on the Global Fund for essential components of its HIV, TB and malaria responses. In 2024, 90pc of HIV financing came from the Fund. This assistance has been invaluable. But indefinite dependence on external financing is neither desirable nor realistic, particularly as international development assistance comes under increasing pressure. Pakistan needs a carefully planned transition towards greater domestic financial responsibility. This does not mean abruptly replacing Global Fund resources or imposing unaffordable obligations on provincial governments overnight. The FCDO-financed, Oxford Policy Management-implemented Global Fund Accelerator Programme is providing valuable analytical support and recommendations. Federal and provincial governments must make optimal use of this opportunity. They should negotiate a gradual increase in domestic financing. Public financing should progressively assume responsibility for recurrent expenditures, while increasingly covering medicines and prevention services. Crucially, exiting ASP and transitioning from donor dependence are related but distinct processes. The Global Fund has stood by Pakistan through successive health emergencies and institutional challenges. Its continued engagement, even after invoking ASP, demonstrates that its objective is not to abandon Pakistan but to protect investments and improve results. Pakistan must respond with the seriousness this partnership deserves. Ultimately, the most compelling argument for reform is not the restoration of international prestige. It is the right of millions of Pakistanis to effective prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The real achievement will be transforming a constrained partnership into a confident, accountable and genuinely country-owned response to three preventable and treatable diseases. The writer is a former health minister, adjunct professor of health systems and population health, president of Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine and convener of Lok Sehat.
articles.author: Zafar Mirza

articles.title: Ambition without scale?
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S newly announcedAuto Policy 2026-31promises cheaper vehicles, higher localisation, exports, employment, improved safety and cleaner transportation. These are worthy objectives. But can they be achieved simultaneously in an industry constrained by limited scale, proliferating makes and models, and the absence of competitive upstream steel, petrochemical and aluminium industries? More importantly, does the policy risk undermining one of the few enduring achievements of decades of automotive protection: the engineering capabilities developed by component manufacturers, with applications in agriculture, defence and other industries? The policy deserves credit for recognising that protection has not delivered internationally competitive vehicles. Gradual tariff reductions, export targets and electric-vehicle incentives signal change. But reducing tariffs without addressing high energy, taxation and financing costs risks weakening domestic manufacturers before they become competitive. Previous auto policies have produced an insufficiently recognised benefit: the engineering capabilities developed by component manufacturers. Guided by international assemblers, Pakistani firms have acquired expertise in precision machining, sheet-metal pressing, plastic moulding, rubber products, glass, wiring and numerous other components. Industrial clusters around Port Qasim, Lahore-Sheikhupura and elsewhere demonstrate capabilities extending beyond automobiles. Losing them would erode an industrial foundation that Pakistan needs for manufacturing diversification and import substitution. Competition among brands is desirable, but proliferation of incompatible platforms undermines supplier competitiveness. Support for technological upgrading, testing and certification is welcome. However, indiscriminate tariff reductions could expose these firms to overseas competitors operating at vastly greater scale, before domestic cost disadvantages are addressed. Protection should neither be indefinite nor unconditional. A differentiated, time-bound approach should preserve engineering capabilities with demonstrable competitive potential, linking support to productivity, quality, scale and exports. Mandatory localisation targets require scrutiny. Components manufactured locally using imported steel, polymers, machinery and tooling cannot reasonably be counted as entirely indigenous. Pakistan lacks integrated automotive-grade steel, petrochemical and aluminium supply chains. The appropriate measure is domestic value addition after deducting imported inputs, including those embedded in locally purchased components. Higher local procurement does not necessarily deliver equivalent foreign-exchange savings. Policy must measure genuine indigenous value addition, technological upgrading and net foreign-exchange contribution separately. Pakistan’s limited vehicle market is increasingly divided among manufacturers, models and variants. Each additional platform can require separate moulds, dies and tooling. Small production runs raise costs and discourage sophisticated manufacturing. Competition among brands is desirable, but proliferation of incompatible platforms undermines supplier competitiveness. Common components, platform sharing, contract manufacturing and supplier consolidation should be encouraged. Pakistan’s motorcycle industry offers an instructive parallel. Standardised designs, large volumes, extensive vendor networks and a substantial replacement market have enabled component manufacturers to develop capabilities while making transportation accessible to millions. Cars require more demanding standards and higher tooling investment, but the lessons of affordability, standardisation and scale remain relevant. Pakistan should encourage one or more safe, fuel-efficient, affordable small-car platforms through collaboration with established international manufacturers. Shared components and higher volumes could support meaningful domestic value addition, strengthen vendors and eventually create export opportunities. Encouraging electric vehicles is appropriate, particularly motorcycles, three-wheelers, small cars and public transport. However, concessional imports of completely built-up vehicles and completely knocked-down kits may accelerate adoption without developing domestic engineering capabilities. The transition should include a roadmap enabling existing component manufacturers to enter EV supply chains. The policy envisages approximately $6 billion in cumulative automotive exports over five years. But who will buy these vehicles? Complete-vehicle exports depend on foreign principals allocating production and overseas markets to Pakistani operations. Such decisions are scale-dependent and cannot be mandated. Potential African and other markets present additional challenges. Pakistan generally lacks preferential trade agreements with these destinations, leaving its vehicles exposed to tariffs while competing against established Asian manufacturers. Export incentives introduce another risk. WTO rules restrict subsidies contingent on export performance, while importing countries can impose countervailing duties following investigations establishing subsidisation and injury. Export targets need identifiable customers, commercial commitments, market access and demonstrated net foreign-exchange earnings. The proposed Automotive Development Levy, expected to raise Rs232bn over five years, raises another question. Pakistan’s experience with the Export Development Fund offers a cautionary lesson. Financed through a levy on exports, it supported various initiatives, but its effectiveness in delivering sustained competitiveness remains debatable. The government’s subsequent decision to review its utilisation, audit its accounts and abolish the surcharge raises legitimate questions about establishing another dedicated levy. Public funding for shared testing facilities, technology transfer and skills development has merit. But taxing consumers to subsidise exports that remain uncompetitive risks replacing tariff protection with another permanent support mechanism. Ultimately, Pakistan must distinguish between assembling vehicles, manufacturing competitive components and providing affordable mobility. These are related but different objectives. The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and the Pakistan Business Council.
articles.author: Ehsan Malik

articles.title: Midterm lessons
articles.content: THERE will be many explanations for the outcome of the US midterm elections. Some will focus on the Iran war, personalities, inflation, tariffs or the divide between Republicans and Democrats. The explanation that interests me most is more fundamental. The US economy was hardly in collapse. The stock market had recently reached unprecedented highs, economic growth remained respectable, unemployment was not a major concern, and overall household wealth had reached high levels by mid-2026. Yet consumer sentiment remained close to record lows, and economic pressure and the cost of living were among the strongest motivations in the election. Growth is no longer enough as a political argument. There is an important message in that contrast. An economy can generate great wealth without large numbers of people feeling that they are becoming better off. This does not mean American voters have rejected capitalism. But it may represent another challenge to an idea that has influenced economic policy for decades; create favourable conditions for business, and the benefits will eventually spread through investment, jobs and higher incomes. There is logic behind part of it. Businesses must make profits. Profitable companies can invest and create employment. What I question is the assumption that business prosperity will automatically become broader prosperity. It may. But it does not have to. Profits can finance new factories and jobs. Technology can raise productivity without producing equivalent growth in employment. This helps explain the apparent contradiction in the US. The stock market can create vast amounts of wealth for those who own financial assets while a worker whose income depends primarily on wages struggles. Many citizens may ask very different questions; am I becoming more economically secure? Can my income keep pace with the cost of living? When enough people become doubtful about those answers, growth begins to lose its political legitimacy. And this is where democracy enters the story. Markets can allocate capital, determine prices and reward economic activity. They cannot decide whether the resulting distribution of wealth, opportunity and security remains acceptable to society. Democracy provides that feedback. When people conclude that the economic bargain no longer works for them, elections provide a peaceful mechanism through which they can demand change. That is the lesson Pakistan should pay attention to. We spend a great deal of time discussing economic stabilisation and growth. Forex reserves improve. Inflation falls. The current account looks better. The stock market rises. All these matter. No economy can prosper for long without macroeconomic stability. But stabilisation and growth are not prosperity. Pakistan has repeatedly gone through cycles in which macroeconomic stabilisation is achieved through adjustment of higher taxes, energy prices, reduced subsidies, tighter spending and slower demand. Some of these measures may be unavoidable. But adjustment is never neutral. Higher taxes reduce disposable income and higher energy prices raise household and business costs. Subsidy cuts hurt those who relied on them, and tighter spending can weaken demand and employment. A society can tolerate considerable inequality and difficult adjustment if people continue to believe that opportunity is open, and the system offers a route towards greater security. It becomes harder when growth appears to occur somewhere else, for somebody else. The lesson from the US midterms is not that capitalism has been rejected. It is that growth is no longer enough as a political argument. The US economy showed that it is possible to have strong growth, low unemployment and extraordinary levels of financial wealth and still have voters deeply dissatisfied with their economic circumstances. Pakistan should take that seriously. Macroeconomic stability is necessary. But Pakistan should be conscious of the timing of the economic model it is now pursuing. Privatisation, deregulation, reducing the state’s commercial footprint and relying more on private enterprise are central to the reform programme. But these are also elements of the market-led economic model that has dominated much of the West for several decades and whose outcomes are now being questioned by voters there. The lesson is not that Pakistan should reject markets. It is that we should not assume that markets, privatisation and growth will by themselves produce broadly shared prosperity. None of them is sufficient if ordinary citizens cannot see a meaningful connection between national economic progress and their own lives. And in a real democracy, eventually they will say so. The writer advises boards and CEOs on strategy, leadership and organisational transformation.
articles.author: Asif Saad

articles.title: Beyond diplomacy
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S relationship with competing global powers, and effective participation in international peace efforts, have offered the country avenues to exercise influence beyond its economic weight. It has managed to grab international attention due to its role as a mediator in facilitating dialogue between the United States and Iran. However, diplomatic recognition does not automatically translate into economic prosperity for a country. Pakistan needs to convert its growing diplomatic relevance into sustainable and durable economic partnerships, which include foreign direct investment, regional connectivity and technology transfer. Pakistan has increasingly sought to use international platforms to seek its economic interests. Its engagements with multilateral forums such as the United Nations, OIC and SCO provide opportunities to promote trade, attract investment and build partnerships. The economic diplomacy initiatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its dedicated coordination with the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) highlight an acknowledgement that economic policy and foreign policy can no longer operate in isolation. Last month, the SIFC presented an investment pipeline to a Senate committee comprising 38 projects with an anticipated investment potential of approximately $40 billion. This is an encouraging indicator of opportunities being pursued. However, this investment pipeline should not be considered the same as realised investment. Investors assess the legal, regulatory and administrative environment in which their investments will operate instead of merely relying on the strength of diplomatic assurances. Constitutional federalism needs to work for economic development. The problem does not simply lie in bureaucratic inefficiency; rather it goes deep into the unresolved question of Pakistan’s federal structure. The 18th Amendment strengthened provincial autonomy by transferring responsibilities from the centre to the provinces. Some of the sectors in which SIFC attracts investments including tourism, agriculture, and minerals require provincial participation as they are outside the mandate of the Federal Legislative List. Therefore, an investment proposal initiated at the federal level may still require provincial approvals and administrative permissions. The SIFC was formulated in 2023 through an amendment in the Board of Investment Ordinance, 2001. However, it is unable to resolve the institutional divide between the centre and provinces on matters related to investment. Section 10E of the Ordinance empowers SIFC to issue recommendations, advice or directions to federal regulatory bodies, public sector entities, authorities and government departments. This section does not expressly extend this directive authority to provincial governments. Such hurdles create an uncomfortable situation for international investors. An investor attracted through assurance of a streamlined approval process and diplomatic engagements may encounter delays once the project reaches the provincial level. The solution does not lie in undermining provincial autonomy or doing expansive interpretation of SIFC’s mandate. Such a solution may give rise to constitutional disputes and alienate provincial governments. The goal should be to make the existing constitutional federalism work for economic development. There are institutional mechanisms that can bridge the divide. The Interprovincial Coordination Committee provides a mechanism for coordination between the federation and provinces. Its mandate includes promoting a uniform approach to matters of common national concern. Investment-related bottlenecks can be formally placed before it. The Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination must transition from its mostly reactive position to an active facilitator of investment-related coordination if this system is to be successful. Another option is provided by the Provincial Investment Committees established under Section 15 of the BOI Ordinance. These committees are meant to support the BOI, promote investment within provinces, and ensure ongoing cooperation with it. They may function as SIFC’s provincial counterparts if properly constituted and operationalised. The Council of Common Interests should continue to be accessible for issues coming under its constitutional purview. It is important, however, to distinguish between ordinary administrative cooperation needed to handle individual investment projects and high-level constitutional and policy disagreements. Ultimately, Pakistan’s diplomatic outreach must be matched by institutional credibility at home. Pakistan cannot ask international investors to place confidence in its economic future while leaving unresolved the question of how its own government will work together to secure that future. The writer is a lawyer based in Islamabad.
articles.author: Laraib Sajid

articles.title: Climate challenges
articles.content: THE poisonous smog blanketing Punjab is an immediate threat to public health, but it also points to a larger environmental crisis that Pakistan can no longer address through piecemeal measures. Lahore’s air quality index stood at ahazardous 358on Wednesday, while other cities struggled under the same toxic haze. Punjab’s government says better monitoring and enforcement have brought improvements over previous years. That is welcome, but the air remains dangerous. While pollution from India compounds the problem, Pakistan must also confront domestic emissions. Moreover, smog is not the country’s only warning. Our climate crises are deeply interconnected. Repeated floods, punishing heatwaves and mounting water stress show how exposed Pakistan is to climate shocks, and how urgently it needs lasting solutions. At COP31, PM Shehbaz Sharifoutlineda cleaner energy future that deserves support. He pointed to nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity added in two years, much of it driven by households seeking relief from expensive electricity. Pakistan has backed a pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy use to 35pc by 2035 and aims for electric vehicles to account for 30pc of new vehicle sales by 2030. These shifts could help reduce fossil-fuel dependence and, especially through cleaner transport, cut harmful emissions. But an energy transition is not, by itself, a climate policy. Pakistan also needs to protect communities from floods and extreme heat, safeguard water supplies and adapt agriculture to changing conditions. The PM rightly called forconcessional financeand affordable technology. Rich industrialised countries bear much of the responsibility for global warming and must help vulnerable nations cope. Yet appeals for international climate justice must run alongside serious action at home. That action requires more than ambitious targets or seasonal restrictions. Authorities must enforce vehicle and industrial emission standards, expand public transport, support farmers in ending crop burning and make clean technology accessible beyond affluent households. Cities must be better prepared for floods and extreme weather, while rural communities need help coping with rising temperatures and water shortages. Federal and provincial governments must work together and ensure that environmental regulations are properly enforced. Businesses, too, must reduce their environmental impact, while citizens have a responsibility to conserve resources, avoid polluting their surroundings and demand action from the state. None of this will be easy in a country facing serious fiscal constraints. But the cost of delay is already being paid in illness, damaged livelihoods and repeated disruption. Pakistan cannot afford to confront its climate crises one disaster, one season and one international summit at a time.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Under fire
articles.content: THE bloodshed continues unabated. On Wednesday, at least 12 policemen weremartyredin the line of duty in KP. Ten lives were lost in an ambush in Kohat while a police party was returning from a clearance operation, and two more were martyred in Swabi when a police patrol cameunder fire. Separately, an explosive-laden pickup slammed into the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, but the attack was promptly repelled. Thankfully, no police casualties were reported in the latter incident. Still, a dozen lives lost in a single day and at least a dozen more injured and hospitalised is a heavy toll for a provincial police force engaged in a relentless, fierce fight against terrorists threatening the state’s writ every day. The Kohat ambush, in particular, appears to have been a major security incident. By police accounts, a team that conducted a joint operation with the civil administration against illegal gold mining in the Darbukach area was returning after completing its objectives when it was ambushed by what appears to have been a very large group. At least 18 attackers were killed as the police fought back. Official data shows that police fatalities and injuries in the first half of this year alone had doubled from the year before. The number of attacks, on the other hand, had risen by 34pc. The data suggests that attacks on police have become increasingly deadly, and, coupled with shortfalls in personnel, arms and necessary equipment, the KP police are increasingly vulnerable as they play a frontline role in ongoing operations against terrorists. Though October saw a marked improvement in the number of attacks compared to just a month earlier, the three incidents on Wednesday underline how fragile those gains can be if the police are not strengthened while the state has the upper hand. After the centretook controlof the province, it bears full responsibility for the police’s protection. The new administration appointed to oversee KP’s affairs must immediately ensure that the provincial security forces receive all the funds they have requested and fill vacant posts on an urgent basis. It must ensure armoured vehicles, protective equipment, night-vision devices and better weapons are supplied to frontline personnel, and that intelligence and army backup are available during police operations in high-risk areas.
articles.author: Editorial
